name: Omar Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI firms, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is your ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play clarinet in a civic orchestra, lead the reed section on rehearsal nights and teach four adults. I have a bachelor’s in music and years of section work, but I am no conservatory professor. I like tuning a rough chord until people hear one another; I dislike the unpaid calls about short advert recordings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work support home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and my wife works at a pharmacy; our children are grown and we still have a mortgage. We have about ten months of expenses saved, my orchestra rate is good and several halls hire around here. I do my own paper diary and have never used AI; a colleague can try it, but I will check my paid call myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the reeds that a quicker office form does not change how we rehearse. I would keep my paper diary and ask for the fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra dates, four pupils and my wife’s wage cover our mortgage. Ten months saved protects us from an ordinary cancelled advert call, so this plateau does not threaten my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep orchestra dates and four pupils, confirm written rehearsal and cancellation fees and request my actual pension estimate. In the first plateau year I would save a fifth of cleared extra concert fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills, without assuming a pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my paid work here. I can plan from a signed concert fee and a pension figure once I receive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI diary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know my paper book and signed sheet, and I have never used AI for these calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you ready to retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot answer that from my age alone. I will request the actual pension estimate and compare it with the mortgage before setting a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hall which paid advert recordings remain and who will listen to the reeds in rehearsal. I would say a generated cue cannot lead a breathing section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect advert buyers to stop paying for some clarinet takes, about a fifth of my income. The orchestra chair may hold for now, but ten months saved cannot replace an ongoing lost fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the orchestra and four pupils and ask for written rates on remaining recordings. After two monthly advert calls disappear, I would seek a posted paid school wind-ensemble director job only if my music bachelor’s and section-leading experience meet its stated requirements, paid live rehearsal and preparation remain, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees; I would check the route and keep current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own recording money shrinking. Nearby schools create possibilities, but I would count an actual post and pay rather than a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a school title alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need paid rehearsal and preparation hours, not a title with volunteer evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to audition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would play for the panel myself. I have never used AI and would not put pupil recordings into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the reeds that thinking AGI could make cheap advert cues around 2028, before robot players arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our short recordings could lose buyers in 2028, and rehearsal preparation might pay less. That would take a noticeable share of my own income even if a robot clarinetist is still three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would keep signed orchestra dates and four pupils. In the first year after 2028, if recordings and preparation fees fall, I would seek a posted paid school wind director role only if its music bachelor’s and leadership requirements fit, actual live teaching and preparation are paid, and a written net offer after travel replaces the loss; I would confirm transport and keep the orchestra and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about that fast fee cut. My savings and nearby employers give me time to read a real vacancy, not a guarantee of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why act before a robot can play?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot clarinetists reach the orchestra pit around 2031, three years after thinking AGI. Recording buyers can switch in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you quit to search full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep each paid orchestra and pupil call until a signed school offer meets the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that thinking AGI around 2031 may make recording work cheap while robot players arrive around 2034. I would ask whether an adult wind group could still book a room at a paid rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me test demand, but I expect short clarinet recordings to bring less money. I would not fill that gap by teaching free on a Saturday or spending our mortgage reserve on a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the orchestra and four pupils and request a written room booking and hire charge before taking fees. After two monthly advert calls disappear, I would offer a separate Saturday adult wind class outside paid orchestra calls only if eight paid places cover my teaching wage and preparation, a paid accompanist, room hire, safe instrument hire and travel; in the first year after 2031 I would repeat only on the same full-cost floor, and if a room or safe instrument fails or fewer than eight pay, I would find a safe replacement at that floor or defer and refund the whole group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing recording pay, though a paid class could partly replace it. A signed wind-class room agreement and eight paid places tell me more than hopeful names on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a hired instrument is unsafe on the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not hand it to a player. I would arrange a safe replacement that preserves the paid floor, or defer and refund every member of the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay an accompanist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They prepare and play with the class, and that is work. Eight fees must cover their wage as well as my teaching, preparation, room, safe instrument hire and travel.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot players around 2039 are separate dates. I would ask the hall to put any future recording-use fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer evening concerts, but I cannot count pension income without an actual estimate. Current orchestra work and my wife’s wage cover the next few years; a decade could still change the recording market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep orchestra dates and four pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save a fifth of cleared extra concert fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months. Before collecting class fees I would get a written room booking and hire charge; if two monthly recordings disappear, in the first year after 2036 I would run a separate adult wind class only when eight paid places cover my teaching and preparation, paid accompanist, room and safe instrument hire and travel outside current calls, repeating on the same floor and replacing unsafe room or instruments or deferring and refunding the whole group if safety or enrolment fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording fees while today’s wages still pay the mortgage. I would read an actual pension statement before changing how many concerts I play.

transcript.speaker: persona

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because recording fees could vanish before any robot enters the pit. Signed live dates, a genuinely paid posted school role and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays a player when a clarinet recording is used again. A recorded clarinet note takes one breath, but the recording can be sold for years.

portrait: Omar is an **experienced clarinetist** with a music bachelor’s, four pupils and well-paid orchestra dates.
He has a **ten-month reserve**, a pharmacy-working wife, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses a **paper diary** and has never used AI for work.
He would test a **paid adult class** only after lost calls and written room, wage and safety terms.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could cut his recording and preparation fees before a replacement job pays.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **signed live dates**, a posted paid school role and written replacement net after travel.
